troubleshootingSteps.action: For a laptop, if the adapter remains completely undetected after driver and BIOS checks, consider a failed internal WiFi card, which in some laptops can be replaced, or use an external USB WiFi adapter as a workaround
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A confirmed hardware failure typically requires either professional replacement of the internal card or a practical external USB alternative

possibleSolutions: Turn off Airplane Mode and check any physical WiFi switch
Enable the WiFi adapter in BIOS/UEFI if disabled
Install the correct WiFi driver from the manufacturer
Replace a failed internal WiFi card or use an external USB WiFi adapter as a workaround
prevention: Keep WiFi drivers updated through official manufacturer channels
Avoid unnecessary BIOS/UEFI changes to hardware settings
Keep a USB WiFi adapter on hand as a backup for critical systems

description: A laptop's battery does not charge when the power adapter is connected, either remaining at the same percentage or continuing to drain despite being plugged in.
symptoms: Battery percentage does not increase while plugged in, or continues to slowly decrease
Windows may show 'Plugged in, not charging' next to the battery icon
Charging indicator light on the laptop, if present, may not illuminate or shows an unusual color/pattern
possibleCauses: Power adapter or charging cable has failed or is not fully connected
Battery has reached the end of its usable life and can no longer hold or accept a charge
Charging port on the laptop is damaged or has debris preventing a proper connection
Battery charge threshold setting intentionally limiting charging to preserve battery health
diagnosticQuestions: Does the power adapter's indicator light, if it has one, show it is receiving power and functioning?
Is the charging cable and connector firmly and fully seated in the laptop's charging port?
Does Windows show 'Plugged in, not charging' or does it not seem to detect being plugged in at all?
Is there any custom battery charge limit software installed or a BIOS setting that might intentionally cap charging at a certain percentage?

commands.purpose: Generate a detailed battery health report including design capacity versus current full charge capacity
commands.expectedResult: Current full charge capacity reasonably close to the battery's original design capacity
commands.abnormalResult: Current full charge capacity significantly reduced from design capacity, indicating significant battery wear or degradation

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm the power adapter and cable are firmly and fully connected at both the wall outlet and the laptop's charging port
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A loose connection is the simplest and most common cause of a laptop not charging

troubleshootingSteps.action: Try a different, known-working power adapter if available, ideally the exact same model or a manufacturer-approved equivalent
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Isolates whether the current adapter itself has failed

troubleshootingSteps.action: Inspect the laptop's charging port for visible damage or debris that might be preventing a proper connection
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Physical damage or blockage in the port is a straightforward cause that can sometimes be visually confirmed

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check for any battery charge limit or 'battery health' software/BIOS setting that might be intentionally capping the charge percentage
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Many modern laptops include a feature to intentionally limit maximum charge to preserve long-term battery health, which can be mistaken for a charging failure

troubleshootingSteps.action: Run a battery health report using powercfg /batteryreport to check the battery's current capacity compared to its original design capacity
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Reveals whether the battery has genuinely degraded significantly, which is a normal outcome of battery aging rather than necessarily a fault

troubleshootingSteps.action: Consider battery replacement if the health report confirms significant capacity loss, or professional inspection if the charging port itself appears physically damaged
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Provides the appropriate path forward depending on whether the root cause is the battery itself or the physical charging connection

possibleSolutions: Reconnect or replace the power adapter/cable
Clean or repair a damaged charging port
Disable an intentional charge limit setting if a higher charge percentage is desired
Replace the battery if significantly degraded
Seek professional repair for a damaged charging port
prevention: Use only manufacturer-approved or certified power adapters
Avoid extreme temperatures when charging, which can accelerate battery wear
Consider using a charge limit feature if available to extend long-term battery lifespan, understanding the trade-off with maximum immediate capacity

description: A laptop's built-in touchpad does not respond to touch, movement, or clicks, preventing normal cursor control without an external mouse.
symptoms: Cursor does not move at all when touching or swiping the touchpad
Tap-to-click or physical click buttons on the touchpad do not register
Touchpad may have worked before and stopped suddenly, or may never have worked on a fresh setup
possibleCauses: Touchpad disabled through a function key combination or in Windows settings
Touchpad driver issue or the device not properly detected
External mouse connected, which automatically disables the touchpad on some laptops by default
Physical hardware failure of the touchpad itself
diagnosticQuestions: Is there a function key combination (often Fn plus a touchpad icon key) that might have accidentally disabled the touchpad?
Is an external mouse currently connected, which some laptops are configured to automatically prioritize over the touchpad?
Does the touchpad work in BIOS/UEFI, indicating a Windows-level rather than hardware-level issue?
Has this touchpad ever worked on this laptop, or has it never functioned since it was new or freshly reinstalled?

commands.purpose: Check whether Windows detects the touchpad as connected hardware, since it is typically classified alongside mice
commands.expectedResult: The touchpad is listed with an 'OK' status
commands.abnormalResult: The touchpad is missing or shown with an error status, indicating a detection or driver-level problem

troubleshootingSteps.action: Try the function key combination commonly used to toggle the touchpad on and off, usually Fn plus a key showing a touchpad icon
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Accidental key presses are a very common and simple cause of a touchpad appearing to stop working entirely

troubleshootingSteps.action: Disconnect any external mouse currently connected, since some laptops are configured by default to disable the touchpad whenever an external mouse is present
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This default behavior is easily mistaken for a touchpad failure when it is actually working as intended

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check Windows Settings under Devices/Touchpad (or Bluetooth & devices > Touchpad) to confirm the touchpad is not disabled there
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Windows has its own separate software toggle for the touchpad that may have been turned off, whether accidentally or by another user

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check Device Manager for the touchpad, typically listed under Mice and other pointing devices, and confirm it is present, enabled, and free of warning icons
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Reveals whether Windows detects the touchpad hardware at all and whether its driver is functioning properly

troubleshootingSteps.action: Update or reinstall the touchpad driver, ideally the manufacturer's specific precision touchpad driver rather than a generic one, including uninstalling and restarting to let Windows reinstall it
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Resolves a corrupted or generic driver that may be preventing full or any touchpad functionality

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the touchpad works in BIOS/UEFI but not in Windows, focus troubleshooting on software/drivers; if it fails even in BIOS/UEFI, this suggests a genuine hardware failure requiring professional repair
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This distinction is critical for correctly directing further troubleshooting effort toward either software or hardware repair

possibleSolutions: Use the function key to re-enable the touchpad
Disconnect an external mouse if it is automatically disabling the touchpad
Enable the touchpad in Windows Settings
Update or reinstall the touchpad driver
Seek professional repair if the touchpad fails even at the BIOS/UEFI level
prevention: Be mindful of function key combinations that toggle the touchpad
Keep touchpad drivers updated through the manufacturer's official support page
Handle the laptop carefully to avoid physical stress on the touchpad's internal connections

description: The desktop power supply unit (PSU) shows no signs of activity when the system is powered on, with no fan spin, no lights, and no response from the system at all.
symptoms: No fan spin, LEDs, or any activity from the PSU when powering on
System is completely unresponsive to the power button
PSU worked previously and stopped suddenly
No activity even when testing the PSU standalone
possibleCauses: PSU switch on the rear of the unit is set to off
Wall outlet or power strip is not providing power
PSU has failed internally
Power cable is damaged or not fully seated
Motherboard short circuit preventing the PSU from starting
diagnosticQuestions: Is the physical switch on the back of the PSU set to the on position?
Has the outlet or power strip been confirmed to have power using another device?
Does the PSU show any activity when tested standalone using a paperclip test?
Was there any recent event, such as a power surge, before this started?

commands.command: PSU paperclip test (jump the green wire to a black ground wire on the 24-pin connector, PSU disconnected from motherboard)
commands.purpose: Test whether the PSU itself can power on independently of the rest of the system
commands.expectedResult: PSU fan spins up, indicating the PSU itself is functional
commands.abnormalResult: PSU shows no activity at all, confirming a PSU-level failure

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm the rear PSU switch is set to on and the outlet/power strip is confirmed working with another device.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Rules out the simplest causes before further diagnosis.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Reseat the power cable at both the wall and PSU ends, or try a different cable.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A damaged or loose power cable can prevent the PSU from receiving power at all.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Disconnect the PSU from the motherboard and perform a paperclip test to check for standalone activity.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Isolates whether the PSU itself is at fault versus a short elsewhere in the system preventing startup.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the PSU shows no activity even standalone, replace the PSU.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Confirms internal PSU failure that cannot be repaired by the end user.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the PSU passes the standalone test but the system still will not power on, investigate a possible short circuit on the motherboard.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A properly functioning PSU that still fails to start the system points to a fault elsewhere in the build.

possibleSolutions: Turn on the PSU's rear power switch
Replace a damaged power cable
Replace a failed PSU
Investigate and resolve a motherboard short circuit
prevention: Use a surge protector to guard against power surges
Periodically inspect power cables for damage
Choose a reputable PSU brand with adequate wattage headroom

description: The system powers on and runs normally, but the fan inside the power supply unit does not spin, raising concerns about PSU cooling and longevity.
symptoms: PSU fan remains still while the system is powered on and running
System otherwise functions normally with no crashes
PSU may feel warmer than usual to the touch
Other case fans and components spin normally
possibleCauses: PSU uses a semi-passive or zero-RPM mode that keeps the fan off under low load
Fan bearing has failed or seized
Dust buildup has jammed the fan blades
Internal fan control circuitry has failed
diagnosticQuestions: Does the PSU specification mention a semi-passive or zero-RPM fan mode?
Does the fan remain still even under heavy system load and high temperatures?
Is there visible dust buildup around the PSU fan grille?
How old is the PSU, and has the fan ever spun normally before?

commands.command: Monitor PSU temperature and fan behavior under sustained heavy load (e.g., stress test)
commands.purpose: Determine whether the fan spins up under high load, which would confirm normal semi-passive operation
commands.expectedResult: Fan spins up as load and temperature increase
commands.abnormalResult: Fan remains still even under sustained heavy load, indicating a genuine fan failure

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check the PSU's specifications to determine if it includes a semi-passive or zero-RPM fan mode.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Many modern PSUs intentionally keep the fan off at low loads, which is expected behavior, not a fault.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Run the system under heavy sustained load, such as a stress test, and observe whether the fan spins up.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Confirms whether the semi-passive threshold is simply not being reached, or the fan genuinely fails to respond to heat.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Power off, unplug, and visually inspect the fan for dust buildup or visible obstruction through the vents.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Dust accumulation can physically prevent the fan from spinning even when commanded to.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the fan remains still under heavy load with no semi-passive mode present, replace the PSU rather than attempting to open and repair it.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: PSUs contain dangerous stored electrical charge and should not be opened by untrained users; replacement is the safe resolution.

possibleSolutions: Confirm semi-passive operation is expected and not a fault
Clean external dust from the PSU vents carefully without opening the unit
Replace the PSU if the fan fails to respond even under heavy load
prevention: Keep the system environment reasonably dust-free
Understand and verify the PSU's fan behavior specifications at purchase
Avoid placing the system in an enclosed, poorly ventilated space

description: The system unexpectedly powers off completely during normal use, without displaying an error message, often suspected to be related to power delivery rather than overheating or software.
symptoms: System powers off abruptly with no warning or blue screen
Shutdown may occur under load, at idle, or seemingly at random
System restarts normally afterward as if nothing happened
No consistent pattern tied to a specific application or task
possibleCauses: Power supply unit is failing or insufficient for the system's power draw under load
Overheating triggering a thermal protection shutdown
Faulty wall outlet or power strip causing intermittent power loss
A failing component, such as RAM or the motherboard, causing a protective shutdown
Windows Fast Startup or power settings causing unexpected sleep/shutdown behavior
diagnosticQuestions: Does the shutdown happen more often under heavy load, such as gaming, or does it seem random?
Has the system's power draw increased recently, such as through a new graphics card?
Has overheating been ruled out as a cause?
Is the system connected to a reliable, tested power outlet or power strip?

commands.command: Event Viewer > Windows Logs > System (filter for Kernel-Power event ID 41)
commands.purpose: Check Windows event logs for a Kernel-Power critical error indicating an unexpected power loss
commands.expectedResult: No unexpected power loss events, or events correlate with known planned shutdowns
commands.abnormalResult: Repeated Kernel-Power Event ID 41 entries with no planned cause, confirming unexpected power loss consistent with a hardware issue

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check Event Viewer for Kernel-Power Event ID 41 entries corresponding to the shutdown times.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This specific event confirms an unexpected loss of power rather than a controlled shutdown or software crash.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Rule out overheating by monitoring CPU and GPU temperatures during normal use leading up to a shutdown.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Thermal protection shutdowns can present identically to power-related shutdowns without careful monitoring.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test the system connected to a different, confirmed-reliable wall outlet.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: An intermittently faulty outlet or power strip can cause exactly this symptom.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Calculate the system's total power draw under load and compare it against the PSU's rated wattage and connector capacity.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: An insufficient or aging PSU unable to meet peak load demand is a very common cause of random shutdowns, especially after a hardware upgrade.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If a spare, known-good PSU of adequate wattage is available, swap it in to test.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: The most reliable way to confirm or rule out the PSU as the root cause.

possibleSolutions: Replace an insufficient or failing PSU with an adequately rated unit
Resolve underlying overheating issues if identified as the actual cause
Use a different, reliable power outlet or power strip
Replace a failing component identified through further isolation testing
prevention: Choose a PSU with adequate wattage headroom for the system's components
Maintain good system cooling to prevent thermal shutdowns
Use a surge protector or UPS for stable power delivery
Recalculate power needs after any significant hardware upgrade

description: The power supply unit emits an audible buzzing, whining, or coil-whine-like noise during system operation, particularly noticeable under certain loads or in quiet environments.
symptoms: High-pitched buzzing or whining noise coming from the PSU area
Noise may intensify under higher system load or specific frame rates in games
Noise may be constant or only present under certain conditions
System otherwise operates normally without crashes or instability
possibleCauses: Coil whine, a common and generally harmless electrical noise from PSU or GPU components under load
PSU fan bearing wear causing a buzzing or grinding sound
Loose internal component within the PSU vibrating against the case
PSU nearing end of life with degrading internal capacitors
diagnosticQuestions: Does the noise change in pitch or intensity based on system load or frame rate?
Is the noise coming specifically from the PSU, or could it be coil whine from the graphics card instead?
Does the system otherwise operate stably with no crashes or errors?
How old is the PSU, and has this noise developed gradually or suddenly?

commands.command: Isolate noise source by testing components individually or listening closely near each component during load
commands.purpose: Determine whether the buzzing noise originates from the PSU specifically or another component like the GPU
commands.expectedResult: Noise source is clearly identified as coming from the PSU
commands.abnormalResult: Noise appears to originate from a different component, redirecting troubleshooting accordingly

troubleshootingSteps.action: Carefully listen near each major component (PSU, GPU) during load to confirm the noise is specifically coming from the PSU.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Coil whine from a graphics card is often mistaken for PSU noise and requires different troubleshooting.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Determine if the noise correlates with load changes, which is characteristic of typical, generally harmless coil whine.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Load-correlated electrical noise is common and usually not a sign of impending failure, providing reassurance if system stability is otherwise fine.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check whether the noise sounds like a mechanical grinding or bearing issue rather than an electrical whine, which would point to the fan instead.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Distinguishes between benign electrical coil whine and a potentially failing PSU fan bearing.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the PSU is older and the noise has developed gradually alongside any signs of instability, consider proactive replacement.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Aging PSUs with degrading components can develop noise as an early warning sign before more serious failure.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the noise is purely electrical coil whine with no instability, no action may be necessary beyond monitoring.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Coil whine, while sometimes annoying, is generally not harmful to the system and does not always require replacement.

possibleSolutions: No action needed if it is confirmed benign coil whine with a stable system
Replace the PSU fan if a mechanical bearing issue is identified
Replace the PSU proactively if age and other symptoms suggest degrading internal components
Address a mistaken GPU coil whine source separately if that is where the noise actually originates
prevention: Choose a reputable PSU brand known for quieter electrical components
Monitor aging PSUs for developing noise or instability
Ensure adequate PSU wattage headroom, as noise can sometimes worsen when a PSU runs near its capacity limit

description: Pressing the case power button produces no response from the system, with no fans, lights, or any indication the system is attempting to start.
symptoms: Pressing the power button has no effect whatsoever
No fans, lights, or beep codes occur when the button is pressed
System can sometimes be started using a different method, such as a motherboard power button
Power button previously worked and stopped functioning
possibleCauses: Power button cable is disconnected or improperly connected to the motherboard front panel header
The power button switch itself has failed
Front panel header pins on the motherboard are bent or damaged
PSU itself is not supplying power at all, unrelated to the button
diagnosticQuestions: Is the front panel power button cable confirmed connected to the correct pins on the motherboard?
Does the system start using a different method, such as directly shorting the power pins with a screwdriver?
Has any recent case or motherboard work been performed that might have disturbed this connection?
Is there any other sign of power reaching the system at all, such as motherboard debug LEDs?

commands.command: Momentarily short the front panel POWER_SW pins on the motherboard using a screwdriver (with system plugged in)
commands.purpose: Test whether the system starts when bypassing the case power button entirely
commands.expectedResult: System powers on successfully when the pins are shorted directly
commands.abnormalResult: System still does not respond, indicating the issue lies elsewhere, such as the PSU or motherboard, rather than the button itself

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm the power button's cable is properly connected to the correct front panel header pins on the motherboard per the manual.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A disconnected or incorrectly placed connector is the most common and simple cause of a non-functional power button.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Momentarily short the POWER_SW pins directly with a screwdriver to test if the system starts, bypassing the case button and cable entirely.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Isolates whether the issue is the button/cable itself or a deeper problem with the motherboard or PSU.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the system starts via the direct short, inspect and test the case power button and its cable for damage or a worn-out switch.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Confirms the fault lies specifically with the physical button or its cable, which can often be replaced independently of the case.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the system does not start even with a direct short, investigate the PSU and motherboard for a power delivery issue.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Indicates the root cause is unrelated to the power button and lies elsewhere in the power chain.

possibleSolutions: Properly reconnect the front panel power button cable
Replace a failed power button switch
Use the direct pin-short method as a temporary workaround
Investigate PSU or motherboard issues if the direct short also fails
prevention: Handle front panel connectors carefully during any case or motherboard work
Document front panel pin layouts for future reference
Test power button function immediately after any hardware changes

description: The system shows absolutely no signs of life when the power button is pressed, with no fans, lights, sounds, or any indication of power reaching any component.
symptoms: Complete absence of fan spin, LED lights, or sound when powering on
No response from motherboard debug LEDs or Q-code displays
Power button and cable have been ruled out as the direct cause
System previously worked normally and stopped suddenly
possibleCauses: PSU has failed completely
Power cable or wall outlet is not delivering power
Motherboard has failed or has a short circuit preventing startup
A component short, such as a failed capacitor, is preventing the PSU from starting
diagnosticQuestions: Has the wall outlet and power cable been confirmed working with another device?
Has the power button and its connection been ruled out as the cause?
Does the PSU show any activity when tested standalone with a paperclip test?
Was there any recent event, such as a power surge or new hardware installation, before this occurred?

commands.purpose: Determine whether the PSU itself is capable of powering on independently
commands.expectedResult: PSU fan spins, confirming the PSU itself is functional
commands.abnormalResult: PSU shows no activity, confirming a PSU-level failure as at least part of the cause

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm the wall outlet and power cable are functional using another known-good device.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Rules out the simplest possible cause before deeper hardware diagnosis.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Rule out the power button itself by directly shorting the POWER_SW pins on the motherboard.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Ensures the issue is not simply a disconnected or faulty power button rather than a genuinely dead system.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Disconnect the PSU from the motherboard and perform a standalone paperclip test.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Isolates whether the PSU itself is functional, separate from any potential motherboard fault.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the PSU passes the standalone test, perform a breadboard test by removing the motherboard from the case and testing with minimal components outside the chassis.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Rules out a case-related short circuit, such as a stray standoff, causing the apparent dead system.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the system still shows no life during a breadboard test with a known-good PSU, the motherboard or CPU is likely at fault and should be tested individually or replaced.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Systematically narrows down the failure to the remaining core components once PSU and case-related causes are ruled out.

possibleSolutions: Replace a confirmed-failed PSU
Replace a damaged power cable
Resolve a case-related short circuit found during a breadboard test
Replace a failed motherboard or CPU identified through systematic isolation
prevention: Use a surge protector or UPS to protect against power events
Handle installation and case work carefully to avoid shorts from stray standoffs or screws
Test major components individually when building or upgrading a system
keywords: no power at all dead system
computer completely dead no lights fans
system will not turn on at all

description: The system appears to power on normally, with fans spinning and lights active, but no image appears on the connected monitor at any point, including during POST.
symptoms: Monitor remains blank or shows a 'no signal' message
System fans and lights indicate the system is powered on
No POST screen, manufacturer logo, or any video output appears
Monitor works fine when tested with a different source device
possibleCauses: Video cable is loose, damaged, or connected to the wrong port
Monitor is set to the wrong input source
Graphics card is not properly seated or has failed
RAM is not properly seated, preventing successful POST
Onboard versus discrete graphics output confusion when both are present
diagnosticQuestions: Has the monitor been confirmed working with another source device?
Is the monitor set to the correct input source matching the connected cable?
Is the cable connected to the graphics card's output specifically, if a discrete card is installed?
Are there any beep codes or debug LED indications suggesting a specific POST failure?

commands.purpose: Read any onboard debug indicators to identify the specific stage of POST failure preventing video output
commands.expectedResult: Debug code indicates successful progress through POST toward video initialization
commands.abnormalResult: Debug code is stuck at an early stage, such as memory or CPU initialization, indicating the video failure is a symptom of an earlier POST failure

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm the monitor works with another source device and is set to the correct input.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Rules out the monitor itself and simple configuration issues before deeper system troubleshooting.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Reseat the video cable at both ends, or try a different cable and port.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Loose or damaged cables are a common and simple cause of no display output.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If a discrete graphics card is installed, confirm the cable is connected to it rather than the motherboard's onboard video output.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This common mix-up produces exactly this symptom when onboard video is disabled or not the active output.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Reseat the RAM modules and graphics card to ensure proper contact.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A POST failure due to improperly seated RAM or a graphics card will prevent any video output from occurring at all.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check for beep codes or motherboard debug LED indicators to identify the specific stage of failure.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Provides a more targeted diagnosis than the generic blank screen symptom alone.

possibleSolutions: Reseat or replace the video cable
Connect to the correct output (discrete card vs onboard)
Reseat RAM and graphics card
Address the underlying POST failure identified via beep codes or debug LEDs
Test with a different graphics card if the current one is suspected faulty
prevention: Use quality, properly seated video cables
Label or note correct output ports when both onboard and discrete graphics are present
Ensure proper seating of all components during any hardware maintenance

description: The connected monitor's image flickers intermittently, ranging from occasional brief flashes to constant rapid flickering, disrupting normal use of the display.
symptoms: Screen flickers or flashes intermittently during normal use
Flickering may worsen under certain conditions, such as specific refresh rates or applications
Issue may affect the entire screen or only parts of it
Flickering persists across different applications and even at the desktop
possibleCauses: Loose or damaged video cable connection
Outdated, corrupted, or incompatible graphics driver
Monitor refresh rate set higher than the cable or monitor can reliably support
Failing monitor backlight or internal component
Graphics card issue, such as overheating or driver instability
diagnosticQuestions: Does the flickering occur with a different cable or connected to a different device?
Was a graphics driver recently updated or changed before the flickering began?
What refresh rate is currently configured, and does lowering it reduce or eliminate the flickering?
Does the flickering happen consistently across all applications, or only in specific ones?

commands.command: Display Settings > Advanced Display > Display Adapter Properties (check current refresh rate)
commands.purpose: Review and test adjusting the currently configured refresh rate as a potential cause
commands.expectedResult: Flickering resolves at a standard, cable-supported refresh rate
commands.abnormalResult: Flickering persists even at a standard refresh rate, pointing to a cable, driver, or hardware cause instead

troubleshootingSteps.action: Reseat the video cable at both ends, or test with a different cable.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A loose or degraded cable connection is one of the most common causes of intermittent flickering.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test the monitor connected to a different device, such as a laptop, to isolate whether the monitor itself is at fault.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Determines whether the flickering follows the monitor or is specific to the original system.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Update or reinstall the graphics driver to the latest stable version from the manufacturer.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Driver issues are a common software-level cause of display flickering that mimics a hardware problem.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Lower the display refresh rate to a standard value, such as 60Hz, to test if flickering resolves.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Some cable and monitor combinations cannot reliably sustain higher refresh rates, causing intermittent flickering.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If flickering persists across different cables, devices, and refresh rates, consider the monitor's backlight or internal components as failing.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Rules out external causes and points toward a genuine monitor hardware failure requiring repair or replacement.

possibleSolutions: Reseat or replace the video cable
Update or reinstall the graphics driver
Lower the display refresh rate to a stable, supported value
Replace the monitor if a hardware failure is confirmed
prevention: Use quality video cables rated for the intended resolution and refresh rate
Keep graphics drivers reasonably up to date
Choose refresh rates that are reliably supported by both the cable and monitor

description: One or more pixels on the monitor display remain permanently a single color (typically black, white, or a bright color) regardless of what content is being shown, indicating a physical panel defect.
symptoms: A specific point on the screen remains the same color across all content
Dead pixel is more noticeable against certain background colors
Number of affected pixels may be a single pixel or a small cluster
Issue is purely visual with no impact on overall monitor function
possibleCauses: A physical defect in the LCD panel present since manufacturing
Pixel damage caused by physical pressure or impact on the screen
A 'stuck' pixel that is misfiring rather than truly dead, which may be recoverable
Panel degradation over the monitor's lifespan
diagnosticQuestions: Is the affected pixel always the same color regardless of what is displayed (dead), or does it flicker between colors (stuck)?
How long has the monitor been in use, and is it still within warranty?
Was there any recent physical impact or pressure applied to the screen?
How many pixels are affected, and where are they located on the screen?

commands.command: Full-screen solid color test pattern (red, green, blue, black, white displayed individually)
commands.purpose: Clearly identify and confirm the location and behavior of the affected pixel(s) against different backgrounds
commands.expectedResult: No inconsistent pixels are visible across all solid color tests
commands.abnormalResult: One or more pixels remain a fixed color inconsistent with the displayed background, confirming a dead or stuck pixel

troubleshootingSteps.action: Display a series of full-screen solid colors to clearly identify whether the pixel is truly dead (always the same color) or stuck (cycling between colors).
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This distinction determines whether pixel-fixing techniques have any chance of resolving the issue.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the pixel appears stuck rather than truly dead, try gentle pixel-massage techniques or dedicated stuck-pixel-fixing software that rapidly cycles colors.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Stuck pixels, unlike truly dead ones, can sometimes be resolved by encouraging the sub-pixel to reset properly.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check the monitor manufacturer's dead pixel policy and warranty status.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Many manufacturers have specific policies about how many dead pixels qualify for a warranty replacement.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If within warranty and the pixel count meets the manufacturer's replacement threshold, initiate a warranty claim.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Provides a path to resolution without cost if the monitor qualifies under the manufacturer's policy.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If out of warranty and pixel-fixing techniques do not help, the monitor may need to be lived with or replaced, as true dead pixels are a permanent hardware defect.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Genuinely dead pixels are a hardware-level display panel defect that cannot be repaired through software or user-level intervention.

possibleSolutions: Attempt stuck-pixel fixing techniques if the pixel is not truly dead
File a warranty claim if the monitor qualifies under the manufacturer's dead pixel policy
Replace the monitor if out of warranty and the defect is significant
Accept minor, isolated dead pixels if they do not significantly impact usability
prevention: Handle and transport monitors carefully to avoid panel impact
Check dead pixel policies before purchasing a monitor
Inspect new monitors promptly upon purchase to catch defects within the return window

description: The system fails to detect or offer the monitor's native or full range of supported resolutions, defaulting to a lower resolution or an incorrect aspect ratio.
symptoms: Available resolution options in display settings do not include the monitor's native resolution
Display appears stretched, blurry, or has incorrect proportions
Only a generic or limited set of resolutions is offered
Issue may have started after a driver update, cable change, or new monitor connection
possibleCauses: Graphics driver is outdated, generic, or not properly installed
Video cable or connection type does not support the monitor's full resolution and refresh rate
Windows is using a generic display driver rather than the monitor's specific EDID information
Monitor's EDID data is not being read correctly by the system
diagnosticQuestions: What is the monitor's actual native resolution according to its specifications?
What resolutions are currently being offered in the display settings?
What type of cable and port is being used to connect the monitor?
Is a proper manufacturer graphics driver installed, or a generic Windows driver?

commands.command: Display Settings > Advanced Display Settings > Display Information
commands.purpose: Check what resolution and refresh rate options the system currently detects for the monitor
commands.expectedResult: Monitor's full native resolution and refresh rate options are available
commands.abnormalResult: Only limited or lower resolution options are shown, confirming a detection issue

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm the monitor's actual native resolution from its specifications or manual.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Establishes the correct target resolution the system should be detecting and offering.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Update the graphics driver to the latest version directly from the manufacturer rather than relying on a generic Windows driver.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Proper manufacturer drivers include more complete EDID handling and resolution support than generic drivers.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test a different video cable or port type, such as switching from HDMI to DisplayPort if available.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Some cable types or older cable versions may not support the bandwidth needed for higher resolutions or refresh rates.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Reinstall the monitor by removing it from Device Manager (under Monitors) and allowing Windows to redetect it.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Forces Windows to re-read the monitor's EDID data, which may resolve a corrupted or incomplete initial detection.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the correct resolution still cannot be selected, manually create a custom resolution matching the monitor's native specifications using the graphics driver's control panel.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Provides a workaround when automatic detection continues to fail despite other troubleshooting.

possibleSolutions: Update to the proper manufacturer graphics driver
Use a different cable or port type with adequate bandwidth
Remove and let Windows redetect the monitor
Manually create a custom resolution matching the monitor's native specs
prevention: Use manufacturer-specific graphics drivers rather than generic ones
Use appropriate cable types for the desired resolution and refresh rate
Verify monitor detection after any cable, driver, or connection changes

description: A laptop or desktop system fails to recognize an externally connected monitor, either showing nothing on the external display or failing to list it as an available display option.
symptoms: External monitor remains blank while the primary display works normally
Display settings do not list the external monitor as detected
External monitor was previously detected and has stopped being recognized
Issue may occur with one specific port or cable type but not others
possibleCauses: Video cable is loose, damaged, or connected to a non-functional port
Laptop's display output mode has not been switched to include the external monitor
Graphics driver issue preventing proper external display detection
Docking station or adapter (for laptops using USB-C/Thunderbolt) is faulty or improperly configured
diagnosticQuestions: Has the external monitor been confirmed working with another source device?
Has the display mode/output key combination (often Windows key + P) been used to select an extended or duplicated display?
Is a docking station, hub, or adapter involved, and has it been tested with a direct connection instead?
Does the issue occur with all ports/cables, or only a specific one?

commands.purpose: Quickly check and select the correct display output mode to include the external monitor
commands.expectedResult: External monitor becomes active when an extend or duplicate mode is selected
commands.abnormalResult: External monitor remains undetected even after selecting an appropriate display mode

troubleshootingSteps.action: Press Windows key + P and select Extend or Duplicate to ensure the external monitor output is enabled.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: The system may simply be configured to show the display only on the primary screen, which resembles a detection failure.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Reseat the video cable at both ends, or test with a different cable and port.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A loose or faulty cable connection is a common and simple cause of external monitor detection failure.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If using a docking station, hub, or adapter, test connecting the monitor directly to the laptop's video output instead.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Isolates whether the intermediate device is the source of the problem rather than the monitor or laptop itself.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Update the graphics driver to the latest version from the manufacturer.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Outdated or corrupted drivers can specifically affect external display detection while leaving the primary display unaffected.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test the external monitor with a different source device to rule out a fault with the monitor itself.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Confirms whether the monitor is genuinely functional before further troubleshooting the source system.

possibleSolutions: Select the correct display mode using Windows key + P
Reseat or replace the video cable
Connect directly, bypassing a faulty docking station or adapter
Update the graphics driver
Replace a confirmed-faulty monitor or adapter
prevention: Use quality cables and adapters rated for the intended resolution
Keep graphics drivers updated, especially after Windows updates
Test external display setups after any driver or Windows update

description: The monitor displays visible horizontal lines or a split appearance during motion, particularly noticeable in fast-moving content like games or video, indicating a synchronization issue between the graphics card and monitor.
symptoms: Horizontal 'tear' lines visible during fast on-screen motion
Effect is most noticeable in games and fast-motion video content
Tearing may worsen at higher or uncapped frame rates
Issue occurs regardless of the specific application in severe cases
possibleCauses: Vertical sync (V-Sync) is disabled, allowing the graphics card to update the frame buffer out of sync with the monitor's refresh cycle
Frame rate significantly exceeds the monitor's refresh rate without frame rate limiting
Adaptive sync technology (G-Sync/FreeSync) is not enabled despite being supported
Graphics driver settings are not properly configured for synchronization
diagnosticQuestions: Is V-Sync currently enabled or disabled in the affected application or graphics driver settings?
Does the monitor support adaptive sync technology such as G-Sync or FreeSync, and is it enabled?
What frame rate is the application achieving compared to the monitor's refresh rate?
Does the tearing occur in all applications, or only specific ones?

commands.command: Graphics driver control panel (NVIDIA Control Panel / AMD Software) > Display/Sync settings
commands.purpose: Review and configure V-Sync and adaptive sync settings globally or per-application
commands.expectedResult: Sync settings are properly configured and screen tearing is eliminated or significantly reduced
commands.abnormalResult: Tearing persists even with sync settings enabled, suggesting a monitor capability or cable limitation

troubleshootingSteps.action: Enable V-Sync within the affected application's graphics settings, if available.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: V-Sync directly addresses screen tearing by synchronizing frame delivery with the monitor's refresh cycle.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check the graphics driver control panel for global or application-specific V-Sync and adaptive sync settings.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Driver-level settings can override or supplement in-application settings and may need to be configured separately.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the monitor supports G-Sync or FreeSync, ensure the feature is enabled in both the monitor's own settings and the graphics driver.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Adaptive sync technologies directly solve tearing by dynamically matching the monitor's refresh rate to the frame rate.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Cap the frame rate at or below the monitor's refresh rate if adaptive sync is not available.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Reduces the mismatch between frame delivery and display refresh that causes tearing, even without full V-Sync.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Verify the cable type and connection supports the necessary bandwidth for adaptive sync features if being used.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Some older cable types or connections may not properly support adaptive sync signaling even if both the GPU and monitor support it.

possibleSolutions: Enable V-Sync in-application or via the graphics driver
Enable G-Sync/FreeSync if supported by the monitor and graphics card
Cap the frame rate at or below the monitor's refresh rate
Use a cable type that properly supports adaptive sync signaling
prevention: Configure sync settings appropriately when setting up a new monitor or graphics card
Use adaptive sync technology where supported for the smoothest experience
Choose appropriate cable types for the monitor's full feature set

description: The monitor displays colors that appear noticeably incorrect, such as an overall tint, washed-out appearance, or specific colors rendering improperly, differing from expected accurate color reproduction.
symptoms: Overall image has an unexpected color tint, such as pink, green, or yellow
Colors appear washed out, oversaturated, or generally inaccurate
Distortion may affect the entire screen or only certain areas
Issue may be constant or intermittent
possibleCauses: Video cable is damaged or not fully seated, affecting specific color signal pins
Monitor color settings, such as color temperature or calibration, have been altered
Graphics driver color settings are misconfigured
Monitor's internal color processing hardware has degraded or failed
External interference or magnetic issue affecting an older CRT-style display (less common with modern LCDs)
diagnosticQuestions: Does the color distortion persist when the monitor is connected to a different source device?
Have any recent changes been made to monitor settings, graphics driver settings, or color profiles?
Does reseating or replacing the video cable have any effect on the distortion?
Is the distortion consistent across the entire screen, or localized to specific areas?

commands.command: Monitor On-Screen Display (OSD) menu > Factory Reset / Color Settings
commands.purpose: Reset the monitor's color settings to factory defaults to rule out a manual misconfiguration
commands.expectedResult: Colors return to accurate, expected appearance after reset
commands.abnormalResult: Color distortion persists even after a factory reset, pointing to a cable, source, or hardware issue

troubleshootingSteps.action: Access the monitor's on-screen display menu and reset color settings to factory defaults.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Rules out manual or accidental misconfiguration of the monitor's own color settings as the cause.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Reseat the video cable at both ends, or test with a different cable.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Damaged cables can specifically affect certain color signal pins, causing a consistent color tint or distortion.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test the monitor connected to a different source device to isolate whether the issue follows the monitor.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Determines whether the distortion is a monitor hardware issue or specific to the original source system's settings or output.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check and reset any custom color profiles or graphics driver color settings on the source system.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Custom color management profiles or driver-level adjustments can cause color distortion independent of the monitor itself.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If distortion persists across cables, sources, and after a factory reset, the monitor's internal color processing hardware is likely failing.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Indicates a genuine hardware fault requiring monitor repair or replacement rather than further configuration changes.

possibleSolutions: Reset the monitor's color settings to factory defaults
Reseat or replace the video cable
Reset graphics driver or system color profile settings
Replace the monitor if a hardware failure is confirmed
prevention: Avoid unnecessary manual adjustments to monitor color settings without documentation
Use quality video cables to prevent signal degradation
Periodically calibrate displays using proper calibration tools for consistent accuracy

description: One or more keys on a keyboard, either built-in or external, fail to register any input when pressed, while other keys continue to function normally.
symptoms: Specific keys produce no character or action when pressed
Issue may affect a single key, a cluster of keys, or an entire row/column
Other keys on the keyboard continue to work normally
Issue may be intermittent or completely consistent
possibleCauses: Debris or dirt lodged under the affected key(s)
Liquid spill damage affecting the keyboard membrane or circuit
Physical damage to the key switch or underlying membrane
Driver or software issue causing the OS to ignore specific key input
A pattern of affected keys suggesting a specific row/column circuit failure on the keyboard matrix
diagnosticQuestions: Does the issue affect a single key, or a pattern such as an entire row or column?
Has there been any recent liquid spill or visible debris near the affected keys?
Does the issue occur consistently, or only intermittently?
Does an external USB keyboard also show the same issue, which would point to a software cause instead?

commands.command: On-Screen Keyboard test (Windows) or online keyboard tester tool
commands.purpose: Test each key individually to precisely map which keys are affected and identify any pattern
commands.expectedResult: All keys register correctly when pressed
commands.abnormalResult: Specific keys fail to register, and any pattern (row/column) becomes clear, helping narrow the cause

troubleshootingSteps.action: Use an online keyboard tester or Windows' On-Screen Keyboard to precisely identify which keys are unresponsive and note any pattern.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A clear pattern, such as an entire row failing, strongly suggests a specific matrix circuit issue rather than random individual key damage.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Power off the device and carefully clean under and around the affected keys using compressed air or, for removable keycaps, gentle removal and cleaning.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Debris is a very common and easily resolved cause of individual key failures.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test with an external USB keyboard if the affected keyboard is built into a laptop.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: If the external keyboard works fine for those same keys, this points to a hardware issue specific to the built-in keyboard rather than a software or driver problem.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check Device Manager for the keyboard and update or reinstall its driver.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Rules out a software or driver-level cause, particularly if all keys on an external keyboard are affected uniformly.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If debris cleaning does not resolve the issue and a clear pattern suggests matrix failure or spill damage is suspected, the keyboard likely requires professional repair or replacement.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Membrane or matrix-level damage typically cannot be resolved through cleaning alone and requires physical repair.

possibleSolutions: Clean debris from under the affected keys
Update or reinstall the keyboard driver
Replace a built-in laptop keyboard if physical damage is confirmed
Use an external keyboard as an immediate workaround while repair is arranged
prevention: Keep liquids away from keyboards
Clean keyboards periodically with compressed air
Use keyboard covers in environments prone to spills or debris

description: Pressing keys on the keyboard produces characters or symbols different from what is printed on the keycap, such as pressing 'Y' and getting 'Z', often due to a language or layout mismatch.
symptoms: Pressed key produces a different, unexpected character
Symbols and punctuation may appear especially incorrect
Issue is consistent across all applications
Physical keyboard layout may not match the printed keycaps
possibleCauses: Windows keyboard input language or layout is set incorrectly, such as QWERTY vs QWERTZ or AZERTY
A regional keyboard layout does not match the physical keyboard's printed layout
Sticky Keys, Filter Keys, or another accessibility feature is altering input unexpectedly
A stuck modifier key (Shift, Ctrl, Alt) is being held down, altering character output
diagnosticQuestions: What operating system language and keyboard layout is currently configured?
Does the physical keyboard's printed layout match the region it was purchased for?
Are any accessibility features like Sticky Keys or Filter Keys currently enabled?
Does the issue occur only with certain keys, such as those affected by punctuation differences between layouts?

commands.command: Settings > Time & Language > Language & region > Keyboard (Windows)
commands.purpose: Review and correct the currently configured keyboard input language and layout
commands.expectedResult: Correct layout matching the physical keyboard is selected and active
commands.abnormalResult: An incorrect or unexpected layout is active, explaining the mismatched character output

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check the currently active keyboard layout in Windows language settings and compare it to the physical keyboard's actual layout.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A mismatched layout, such as QWERTY selected for a QWERTZ physical keyboard, is the most common cause of this exact symptom.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Change the keyboard layout setting to match the physical keyboard, or add and switch to the correct layout if not already installed.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Directly resolves the mismatch by aligning software input mapping with the physical keys.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check for and disable Sticky Keys, Filter Keys, or other accessibility features that may be altering input unexpectedly.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: These features can sometimes cause unexpected character behavior that resembles a layout mismatch.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test pressing each modifier key individually to check for a physically stuck Shift, Ctrl, or Alt key.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A stuck modifier key held down can alter character output in ways that mimic a layout issue.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test with a different keyboard to rule out a hardware-specific fault causing incorrect key mapping.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Helps confirm whether the issue is purely software/layout related or involves a hardware fault with the specific keyboard.

possibleSolutions: Correct the keyboard layout setting to match the physical keyboard
Disable interfering accessibility features
Clean or repair a physically stuck modifier key
Replace the keyboard if a hardware mapping fault is confirmed
prevention: Verify keyboard layout settings match the physical keyboard when setting up a new system
Be cautious when installing additional language/keyboard layouts to avoid accidental switching
Keep keyboards clean to prevent stuck modifier keys

description: One or more physical keys on the keyboard feel stiff, slow to return, or remain physically depressed after being pressed, causing repeated characters or missed keystrokes.
symptoms: A key feels noticeably stiffer or slower to return than other keys
Key remains physically depressed after release in severe cases
Repeated or duplicate characters appear when the affected key is pressed
Physical resistance or a grinding feeling when pressing the key
possibleCauses: Liquid spill residue causing the key mechanism to stick
Dust, debris, or crumbs lodged under or around the key
Physical wear or damage to the key's internal switch mechanism
The keycap itself is misaligned or not properly seated on its stem
diagnosticQuestions: Was there any recent liquid spill or food debris near the affected key?
Does the key feel physically different (stiffer, slower) compared to unaffected keys, or does it register but produce wrong output?
Is this an isolated single key issue, or are multiple keys affected similarly?
Has the keycap been recently removed and reinstalled, possibly misaligned?

commands.command: Physical inspection and manual key press test
commands.purpose: Directly observe the affected key's physical movement and resistance compared to unaffected keys
commands.expectedResult: Key moves freely and returns immediately like other keys
commands.abnormalResult: Key shows noticeable resistance, slow return, or remains partially depressed, confirming a mechanical sticking issue

troubleshootingSteps.action: Power off the device and carefully remove the affected keycap, if it is a removable type, following proper technique to avoid damaging the retention clips.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Provides access to clean and inspect the underlying key mechanism directly.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Clean the exposed key switch and surrounding area using compressed air and, if needed, a small amount of isopropyl alcohol on a cotton swab for sticky residue.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Removes debris or dried liquid residue that is likely causing the mechanical resistance.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Allow the area to fully dry before reinstalling the keycap, ensuring it is properly aligned with its stem.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A misaligned keycap reinstallation can itself cause a sticking sensation even after successful cleaning.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test the key's movement and responsiveness after reinstallation.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Confirms whether the cleaning and realignment resolved the physical sticking issue.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the key remains stuck or sticky after cleaning, the internal switch mechanism may be damaged and require replacement of that key switch or the keyboard itself.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Persistent mechanical issues despite cleaning indicate a deeper physical failure of the switch itself.

possibleSolutions: Clean the key switch and surrounding area of debris or residue
Properly realign a misaligned keycap
Replace an individual key switch if repairable (mechanical keyboards)
Replace the keyboard if damage is severe or unrepairable
prevention: Keep liquids and food away from keyboards
Clean keyboards regularly with compressed air
Handle keycaps carefully during any removal or cleaning

description: An externally connected keyboard, whether wired or wireless, is not recognized by the system, producing no input response despite being properly connected or paired.
symptoms: No response from the system when typing on the external keyboard
Keyboard's LED indicators, if present, may or may not light up
Keyboard does not appear in Device Manager
Issue may be specific to one USB port or occur across all ports
possibleCauses: USB connection is loose, damaged, or connected to a non-functional port
Wireless keyboard's receiver dongle is not properly connected or paired
Wireless keyboard batteries are depleted
Driver issue preventing the keyboard from being recognized
Keyboard itself has failed
diagnosticQuestions: Is this a wired or wireless keyboard, and if wireless, are the batteries confirmed fresh?
Does the keyboard work when tested on a different system?
Does switching to a different USB port change the behavior?
For wireless keyboards, is the USB receiver dongle properly connected, and has re-pairing been attempted?

commands.purpose: Check whether Windows detects the external keyboard as connected hardware, even if it is not functioning correctly
commands.expectedResult: Keyboard is listed with an 'OK' status
commands.abnormalResult: Keyboard is missing entirely or shown with an error status, indicating a detection or driver-level problem

troubleshootingSteps.action: For wired keyboards, reseat the USB connection or try a different USB port and cable if possible.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A loose or faulty USB connection is the most common and simple cause of a wired keyboard not being detected.

troubleshootingSteps.action: For wireless keyboards, replace the batteries and confirm the USB receiver dongle is properly and fully connected.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Depleted batteries or a loose receiver are very common causes of wireless keyboard detection failure.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Attempt to re-pair the wireless keyboard with its receiver following the manufacturer's pairing procedure.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Resolves cases where the pairing connection has been lost or corrupted.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check Device Manager to see if the keyboard is detected at all, even without full functionality.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Distinguishes between a complete hardware detection failure and a driver-level issue.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test the keyboard on a different system to determine if the keyboard itself is faulty versus an issue specific to the original system.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Definitively isolates whether the keyboard hardware or the original system is the source of the problem.

possibleSolutions: Reseat or replace the USB cable/connection
Replace batteries in a wireless keyboard
Re-pair the wireless keyboard with its receiver
Update or reinstall the keyboard driver
Replace the keyboard if confirmed faulty via testing on another system
prevention: Keep spare batteries on hand for wireless keyboards
Use quality USB cables and avoid excessive strain on connectors
Periodically check wireless pairing stability

description: The system produces no audio at all through any connected speakers or headphones, despite the operating system appearing to function normally otherwise.
symptoms: No sound plays through speakers or headphones from any application
Volume controls appear to function but produce no audible result
System volume icon may show as muted or at an unusually low level
Sound worked previously and stopped suddenly, or has never worked on a fresh setup
possibleCauses: System volume is muted or set very low
Incorrect audio output device is selected as default
Audio driver is missing, outdated, or corrupted
Physical connection issue with speakers or headphones
Audio hardware itself has failed
diagnosticQuestions: Is the system volume confirmed unmuted and set to an audible level?
Is the correct output device selected as the default playback device?
Does the issue affect all audio output devices, or only a specific one such as headphones?
Did this begin after any recent Windows update, driver change, or hardware change?

commands.command: Settings > System > Sound (check output device and volume)
commands.purpose: Confirm the correct output device is selected and volume is properly configured
commands.expectedResult: Correct device is selected with appropriate volume, and a test sound plays audibly
commands.abnormalResult: Wrong device is selected, or volume is muted/very low, or the test sound still fails to play

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm system volume is unmuted and at an audible level, and test using the built-in sound test.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Rules out the simplest and most common causes before deeper investigation.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Verify the correct audio output device is selected as the default playback device in sound settings.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Audio may be playing correctly but routed to an unexpected or disconnected output device.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check physical connections for wired speakers or headphones, ensuring cables are fully seated in the correct ports.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A loose or incorrect physical connection is a common and simple cause of no audio output.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Update or reinstall the audio driver from the manufacturer's official source.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A missing, outdated, or corrupted audio driver is a frequent cause of complete audio failure.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Run the Windows built-in audio troubleshooter for additional automated diagnostics and fixes.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Can catch and resolve common configuration issues not immediately obvious through manual inspection.

possibleSolutions: Unmute and adjust system volume appropriately
Select the correct default audio output device
Reseat or replace speaker/headphone connections
Update or reinstall the audio driver
Replace failed audio hardware if confirmed through testing
prevention: Check audio settings after Windows updates or driver changes
Keep audio drivers reasonably up to date
Handle audio cables and connectors carefully to avoid damage

description: A connected or built-in microphone fails to pick up audio, either not being detected at all or producing no audible input during calls, recordings, or voice applications.
symptoms: Other participants in a call report they cannot hear the user at all
Recording or voice applications show no input level activity
Microphone does not appear in the list of available input devices
Microphone worked previously and stopped functioning
possibleCauses: Microphone is muted at the system, application, or physical hardware level
Incorrect input device is selected as the default microphone
Microphone privacy/permission settings are blocking application access
Driver issue preventing proper microphone detection or function
Physical connection issue or hardware failure
diagnosticQuestions: Is the microphone confirmed unmuted at the system, application, and any physical mute switch level?
Is the correct microphone selected as the default input device?
Have microphone privacy/permission settings been checked for the affected application?
Does the microphone work in one application but not another, suggesting an app-specific permission issue?

commands.purpose: Check whether microphone access is enabled system-wide and for the specific application experiencing issues
commands.expectedResult: Microphone access is enabled for the system and the relevant application
commands.abnormalResult: Microphone access is disabled for the system or specific application, explaining the lack of input

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm the microphone is not muted at the system level, within the specific application, and via any physical mute switch or button.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Muting can occur at multiple levels, and any one of them being active will fully block audio input.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Verify the correct microphone is selected as the default input device in system sound settings.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Multiple audio input devices being present can lead to the wrong one being selected, especially after connecting new hardware.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check microphone privacy settings to ensure both the system and the specific application have been granted access.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Modern operating systems require explicit permission for applications to access the microphone, which is easy to overlook.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test the microphone input level directly in system sound settings while speaking to confirm whether any signal is being received at all.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Determines whether the issue is a detection/permission problem or the microphone genuinely is not picking up any audio.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Update or reinstall the audio driver, and test the microphone on a different system if a hardware fault is suspected.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Addresses driver-level causes and helps isolate a genuine hardware failure from a software configuration issue.

possibleSolutions: Unmute the microphone at all relevant levels
Select the correct default input device
Grant microphone access in privacy settings for the system and application
Update or reinstall the audio driver
Replace the microphone if a hardware fault is confirmed
prevention: Review microphone privacy settings after major OS updates
Label or note physical mute switches on external microphones
Test microphone function before important calls or recordings

description: Audio output through speakers or headphones is accompanied by crackling, popping, static, or general distortion, degrading the listening experience even though sound is otherwise present.
symptoms: Audible crackling, popping, or static noise mixed with normal audio
Sound may cut in and out or stutter intermittently
Distortion may worsen at higher volumes or during specific types of audio
Issue may be constant or intermittent
possibleCauses: Audio driver issue or outdated driver causing processing glitches
Loose or damaged audio cable connection
Audio enhancements or effects causing processing artifacts
System resource strain causing audio buffer underruns
Failing audio hardware, such as a degrading DAC or speaker driver
diagnosticQuestions: Does the crackling occur with all audio sources and applications, or only specific ones?
Does the issue persist when using a different set of speakers or headphones?
Are any audio enhancements or effects currently enabled in sound settings?
Does the crackling correlate with high system resource usage, such as during heavy multitasking?

commands.command: Sound Control Panel > Playback Device Properties > Enhancements tab
commands.purpose: Check whether audio enhancements are enabled, which can sometimes cause processing artifacts
commands.expectedResult: Enhancements are disabled or not causing any distortion
commands.abnormalResult: Enhancements are enabled and disabling them improves or resolves the crackling

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test with a different set of speakers or headphones to determine if the issue follows the original output device.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Isolates whether the problem lies with the specific audio output hardware or elsewhere in the system.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Disable audio enhancements and effects in the playback device properties.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Enhancement processing can sometimes introduce artifacts, especially with certain driver versions or hardware combinations.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Update or reinstall the audio driver to the latest stable version.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Driver bugs are a common cause of audio processing glitches that manifest as crackling or distortion.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check system resource usage during audio playback to see if high CPU load correlates with the crackling.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Resource-starved audio processing can cause buffer underruns that produce exactly this kind of intermittent distortion.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Reseat or replace the audio cable connection, and test with a different port if available.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Physical cable or connection issues can introduce interference or signal degradation resulting in crackling.

possibleSolutions: Disable audio enhancements causing artifacts
Update or reinstall the audio driver
Address high system resource usage during audio playback
Reseat or replace the audio cable connection
Replace failing audio hardware if confirmed via testing
prevention: Keep audio drivers updated to stable, tested versions
Avoid unnecessary audio enhancement processing unless specifically desired
Monitor system resource usage during audio-intensive tasks

description: A Bluetooth speaker, headphone, or headset fails to pair or maintain a connection with the system, either failing initial pairing or repeatedly disconnecting during use.
symptoms: Bluetooth device does not appear in the list of available devices during pairing
Pairing attempt fails or times out
Device pairs successfully but disconnects frequently during use
Audio device connects but no sound routes through it
possibleCauses: Bluetooth is disabled on the system
Device is not in pairing mode or has a stale pairing record needing removal
Bluetooth driver is outdated or malfunctioning
Interference from other wireless devices affecting connection stability
Audio device battery is low, causing connection instability
diagnosticQuestions: Is Bluetooth confirmed enabled on the system?
Has the audio device been placed in pairing mode correctly per its manual?
Is there an existing, possibly corrupted pairing record for this device that should be removed and re-paired?
Is the audio device's battery confirmed to be adequately charged?

commands.purpose: Check Bluetooth status and manage existing device pairings, including removing stale entries
commands.expectedResult: Bluetooth is enabled and the device can be successfully paired or reconnected
commands.abnormalResult: Bluetooth is disabled, or the device fails to pair/connect even after troubleshooting steps

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm Bluetooth is enabled on the system and the audio device is charged and in proper pairing mode.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Addresses the most basic and common prerequisites for a successful Bluetooth connection.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Remove any existing pairing record for the device from Bluetooth settings, then attempt to re-pair from scratch.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A stale or corrupted pairing record is a common cause of connection failures even when the device appears in range.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Move the device closer to the system and away from other wireless devices or sources of interference.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Distance and interference from other 2.4GHz devices can prevent successful pairing or cause connection instability.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Update the system's Bluetooth driver to the latest version from the manufacturer.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Outdated or buggy Bluetooth drivers are a frequent cause of pairing and connection stability issues.

troubleshootingSteps.action: Test the audio device pairing with a different system to determine if the device itself is at fault.
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Isolates whether the problem lies with the audio device or is specific to the original system's Bluetooth hardware or software.

possibleSolutions: Enable Bluetooth and ensure the device is properly in pairing mode
Remove the stale pairing and re-pair from scratch
Reduce distance and interference during pairing
Update the Bluetooth driver
Replace the audio device if confirmed faulty via testing on another system
prevention: Keep Bluetooth drivers updated
Periodically clear unused or old Bluetooth pairings
Keep audio devices adequately charged

description: A specific USB port on the system fails to recognize any connected device, while other USB ports on the same system function normally.
symptoms: No devices are ever detected when connected to this specific port
Multiple different, known-good devices fail when connected to this port
The same devices work correctly when connected to a different USB port
Port may show no power indication, such as not charging a phone
possibleCauses: Physical damage to the USB port connector
Port is disabled in BIOS or Device Manager
Internal USB header connection (for front-panel ports) is loose or disconnected
USB controller driver issue affecting that specific port or header
Motherboard-level USB port or controller failure
diagnosticQuestions: Does the issue occur with multiple different devices, or just one specific device?
Does the same device work correctly when connected to a different USB port?
Is this a front-panel port that connects via an internal header, and has that header connection been checked?
Is there any visible physical damage to the port itself?

commands.command: Device Manager > Universal Serial Bus controllers
commands.purpose: Check for any USB controllers or hubs showing errors that might correspond to the affected port
