possibleCauses: The background service crashed due to an unexpected error
The service was manually stopped for maintenance and not yet restarted
A dependency required by the service, such as a database connection, became unavailable
A recent update or configuration change caused the service to fail to start properly
The server hosting the service ran out of necessary resources, causing it to stop
diagnosticQuestions: What specific automated or scheduled function seems to have stopped working?
When was the last time this specific function worked correctly?
Have you received any communication about planned maintenance affecting background services?
Are other features of the application, not related to this specific background process, still working normally?

troubleshootingSteps.action: Identify exactly which specific automated or scheduled function has stopped working, distinguishing it from general application access
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This helps clarify that the issue is specifically with a background service rather than the entire application being down

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm that other parts of the application, unrelated to this specific background function, continue to work normally
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This helps isolate the problem specifically to the affected service rather than a broader application-wide outage

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check for any recent communication from IT about planned maintenance that might explain a temporarily stopped service
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Background services are sometimes intentionally paused during maintenance windows, which would explain the temporary disruption

troubleshootingSteps.action: Note the exact time the affected function was last known to work correctly, and any specific error messages or notifications related to it
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This information is important for the administrator to correlate with server logs and identify exactly when and why the service stopped

troubleshootingSteps.action: This type of issue generally cannot be resolved directly by an end user, since it involves restarting or repairing a backend service
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Background services typically require server-level administrative access to properly diagnose, restart, or repair

troubleshootingSteps.action: Report the specific stopped function, along with all gathered details, to the system administrator as a priority issue
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Prompt reporting with specific details helps the administrator quickly identify and restart the affected service, minimizing business impact

troubleshootingSteps.action: Once the administrator confirms the service has been restarted, verify that the previously affected function is now working correctly again
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This confirms the issue has been fully resolved and the automated process is functioning as expected once more

possibleSolutions: Wait out a known, planned maintenance window affecting the service
Report the specific stopped service to the system administrator with detailed timing information
Have the administrator restart or repair the affected background service
Verify full functionality once the administrator confirms the service is restored
prevention: Stay informed of scheduled maintenance affecting background services
Report stopped automated functions promptly with specific details
Maintain monitoring and alerting for critical background services where possible

description: The user tries to access a company website or web-based application through their browser, but the page fails to load entirely, showing a browser-level error rather than any part of the website itself.
symptoms: Browser shows an error such as 'This site can't be reached' or 'DNS_PROBE_FINISHED'
The page never begins to load, showing only a browser error page
Problem may happen with just this one website, or several
Other websites may load normally at the same time
possibleCauses: A DNS resolution problem preventing the website's address from being found
No active internet or network connection
The website's server is down or unreachable
A firewall or content filtering system blocking access to the site
An incorrect URL was typed or bookmarked
diagnosticQuestions: What exact error message does the browser show?
Are other websites loading normally on the same computer and network right now?
Have you successfully accessed this specific website before from this location?
Are you on the company network, a home network, or a public network?

commands.purpose: Test basic network connectivity to the website's server
commands.expectedResult: Replies received from the server
commands.abnormalResult: Request timed out or 'could not find host', indicating a network or DNS resolution problem

commands.purpose: Clear the local DNS cache in case it contains outdated or corrupted information for this website
commands.expectedResult: Confirmation that the DNS cache was successfully flushed
commands.abnormalResult: An error appears, which is uncommon but may indicate a deeper network configuration issue

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm other websites load normally on the same computer and network
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This determines if the problem is specific to this one website, or a broader internet connectivity issue

troubleshootingSteps.action: Double-check the website address for any typing mistakes, comparing it against a known correct source if possible
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A simple typo in the URL is a common and easily overlooked cause of a website failing to load

troubleshootingSteps.action: Ping the website's address to test basic network connectivity to its server
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This helps distinguish between a DNS resolution problem and the website's server itself being unreachable

troubleshootingSteps.action: Flush the local DNS cache using ipconfig /flushdns, then try loading the website again
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This clears any outdated or corrupted cached DNS information that might be preventing the correct address from being found

troubleshootingSteps.action: Try accessing the website from a different device or network, such as a mobile phone using cellular data
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This helps determine if the problem is specific to your original computer and network, or affects the website more broadly

troubleshootingSteps.action: If on a company or public network, consider that a firewall or content filtering system may be intentionally blocking access to this specific website
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Many organizations implement web filtering that can block certain categories of websites, which would explain a consistent failure to load

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the website is a known company resource and appears genuinely down for everyone, report it to the system administrator, including the exact error message and website address
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This provides the administrator with specific information needed to investigate a potential hosting or DNS configuration issue on their end

possibleSolutions: Correct a mistyped website address
Flush the local DNS cache
Confirm broader internet connectivity is working
Test access from a different device or network
Report a confirmed company website outage to the system administrator
prevention: Bookmark frequently used website addresses to avoid typing mistakes
Keep DNS settings properly configured
Report website access issues promptly with specific error details

problem: Cannot access a shared folder used by the application
description: The application relies on a shared network folder for storing or retrieving certain files, but the user or the application itself cannot access this shared location, causing related features to fail.
symptoms: Error message referencing an inaccessible shared folder or network path
Features relying on file storage, such as attachments or exports, fail specifically
The main application interface may still work normally otherwise
Problem may affect one user or several people relying on the same shared folder
possibleCauses: The computer hosting the shared folder is turned off or disconnected from the network
The user's account lacks the correct permissions to access the shared folder
The shared folder path has changed or been moved without updating the application's configuration
A network connectivity problem between the user's computer and the shared folder location
File and printer sharing settings are disabled on the hosting computer
diagnosticQuestions: Do you know where this shared folder is physically located, such as on a specific server or another user's computer?
Have you been able to access this shared folder successfully before?
Are other users experiencing the same issue accessing this shared location?
Is the computer or server hosting this shared folder currently powered on and connected to the network?

commands.command: ping [shared folder host computer name or IP]
commands.purpose: Check if the computer hosting the shared folder is reachable on the network
commands.expectedResult: Replies received from the host computer
commands.abnormalResult: Request timed out, meaning the host computer is off, disconnected, or unreachable

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm the computer or server hosting the shared folder is turned on and connected to the network
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A shared folder is only accessible while its hosting computer is running and properly connected

troubleshootingSteps.action: Ping the host computer or server to confirm basic network reachability
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This verifies whether a network path currently exists to the location hosting the shared folder

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check with other users who rely on the same shared folder to see if they are experiencing the same access problem
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This helps determine if the issue is specific to your account and permissions, or reflects a broader problem with the shared folder itself

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm you have the correct permissions to access this specific shared folder, checking with the folder owner or IT if uncertain
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Insufficient permissions will prevent access even when the shared folder itself is otherwise online and functioning correctly

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the application specifically references a shared folder path in its configuration, confirm this path is still correct and has not changed
troubleshootingSteps.reason: If the shared folder was moved or renamed, the application's stored path reference would become outdated and no longer work

troubleshootingSteps.action: Try accessing the shared folder directly through File Explorer, outside of the application, to isolate whether the problem is with general network access or specific to the application's configuration
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This helps determine if the issue is a broader network/permissions problem, or specifically related to how the application is configured to reach the folder

troubleshootingSteps.action: Report the issue to the system administrator, providing the specific shared folder path and the exact error message experienced
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Correcting an application's configured path, or a shared folder's underlying permissions or availability, typically requires administrator-level access

possibleSolutions: Restore power and network connectivity to the shared folder's host computer
Request corrected access permissions for the shared folder
Update the application's configuration if the folder path has changed
Confirm broader network access to the shared location outside the application
Report configuration or permission issues to the system administrator
prevention: Keep shared folder host computers powered on and connected during business hours
Document and communicate shared folder path changes proactively
Confirm proper permissions are set up when shared folders are first configured
Regularly verify shared folder accessibility for critical application functions

description: An update to the application, whether a desktop client or a scheduled system-wide update, fails to install correctly, potentially leaving the application in an inconsistent or non-functional state.
symptoms: Error message during the update installation process
Update appears to install but the application still shows the old version
The application becomes unstable or fails to open after a failed update attempt
Update process gets stuck partway through and does not complete
possibleCauses: Insufficient permissions to install updates on the computer
A network interruption during the update download or installation process
Insufficient disk space to complete the update installation
A conflict with existing files or a previous incomplete update
The update package itself is corrupted or was not fully downloaded
diagnosticQuestions: What exact error message, if any, appears during the failed update attempt?
Do you have administrator rights on this computer, if required for installing updates?
How much free disk space is currently available on this computer?
Did the update installation process get interrupted, such as by a lost network connection or a forced computer restart?

troubleshootingSteps.action: Note the exact error message or behavior observed during the failed update attempt
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Specific error details help narrow down whether the cause is related to permissions, disk space, or a corrupted update package

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm you have the necessary administrator permissions on the computer to install updates, if required by this specific application
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Insufficient permissions are a common and straightforward cause of failed installation attempts for desktop applications

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check available free disk space on the computer, since updates require sufficient room to download and install properly
troubleshootingSteps.reason: An update can fail partway through if there is not enough free space to complete the installation process

troubleshootingSteps.action: Free up disk space if it is low, then attempt the update again
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This directly addresses a lack of storage space, which is required for many update installations to complete successfully

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm your network connection remained stable throughout the update download and installation process, and retry if it was previously interrupted
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A dropped connection during download or installation is a common cause of a corrupted or incomplete update

troubleshootingSteps.action: Restart the computer completely before attempting the update again
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This clears any temporary file locks or system state issues left over from the previous failed attempt

troubleshootingSteps.action: If a previous update attempt left the application in an unstable state, consider whether a repair or reinstall of the application is needed before attempting the update again
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A partially completed previous update can sometimes prevent a fresh update attempt from succeeding until the application is returned to a clean, stable state

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the update continues to fail despite these steps, contact the system administrator or IT support, providing the exact error message and steps already attempted
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Persistent update failures may require administrator-level tools or a manually managed installation to properly resolve

possibleSolutions: Obtain necessary administrator permissions before installing
Free up disk space before retrying the update
Ensure a stable network connection throughout the update process
Restart the computer before retrying a failed update
Repair or reinstall the application if a previous update left it unstable
Contact IT support for persistent update failures
prevention: Ensure adequate free disk space is maintained regularly
Maintain a stable network connection during scheduled update windows
Avoid interrupting update installations once started
Keep administrator credentials available for systems requiring them for updates

description: The computer does not start Windows normally. It may show a black screen, an error message, or simply never reach the login or desktop screen no matter how long it is left running.
symptoms: Computer powers on but Windows never loads
Black screen with just a mouse cursor, or nothing at all
Error message about a missing operating system
Computer restarts on its own before reaching the desktop
possibleCauses: Corrupted or missing system boot files
The hard drive or SSD has failed or is not detected
A recent update or driver installation broke startup
The boot order in BIOS/UEFI is set to the wrong device
Loose internal cables (for desktop computers)
Malware damaging critical startup files
A failing power supply not providing stable power
diagnosticQuestions: What exactly do you see on the screen when you try to turn it on?
Did anything happen right before this started, like a power outage, update, or new hardware?
Does the computer make any beep sounds or show any error codes?
Have you tried restarting more than once?
Is this a desktop or laptop computer?

commands.purpose: Repair the master boot record from Windows Recovery Environment
commands.expectedResult: Command completes successfully with 'The operation completed successfully'
commands.abnormalResult: An error appears, meaning the boot record damage may be more serious or the drive is not accessible

commands.purpose: Scan for Windows installations and rebuild the boot configuration data
commands.expectedResult: Finds the Windows installation and offers to add it to the boot list
commands.abnormalResult: Reports 'Total identified Windows installations: 0', meaning Windows files cannot be found or the drive has a problem

troubleshootingSteps.action: Note exactly what appears on screen, including any error codes or messages
troubleshootingSteps.reason: The exact symptom points to very different causes, such as a hardware failure versus a software boot problem

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check that all internal cables (power and data) are firmly connected, if this is a desktop computer that was recently moved or opened
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A loose drive cable can make Windows appear to fail to boot when the real issue is the drive not being detected at all

troubleshootingSteps.action: Enter the BIOS/UEFI settings and confirm the correct drive is set as the first boot device
troubleshootingSteps.reason: If the boot order changed, the computer may be trying to start from the wrong device

troubleshootingSteps.action: Boot from Windows installation media or a recovery drive to access Windows Recovery Environment
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This gives access to repair tools that are not available from a normal broken boot

troubleshootingSteps.action: Run Startup Repair from the recovery environment
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This automated tool detects and fixes many common boot problems without manual commands

troubleshootingSteps.action: If Startup Repair does not fix it, run bootrec /fixmbr and bootrec /rebuildbcd from the recovery command prompt
troubleshootingSteps.reason: These commands directly repair the boot files that tell the computer how to start Windows

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the drive is not detected at all in BIOS or recovery tools, this points to a failed or disconnected drive rather than a software issue
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Software repair tools cannot fix a drive that the computer cannot even see

possibleSolutions: Reconnect loose internal cables
Correct the boot device order in BIOS/UEFI
Run Startup Repair from Windows Recovery Environment
Rebuild the boot configuration using bootrec commands
Replace a failed hard drive or SSD
Reinstall Windows if boot files cannot be repaired
prevention: Avoid sudden power loss during Windows updates
Use a UPS (battery backup) for desktop computers
Keep a Windows recovery drive prepared in advance
Avoid interrupting the computer during shutdown or updates

problem: Computer is stuck on the Windows loading screen
description: When starting the computer, the Windows logo and spinning dots appear as normal, but the computer stays on this screen for a very long time or forever, never reaching the login screen.
symptoms: Windows logo with spinning dots stays on screen for many minutes
No error message appears, the computer just does not move forward
Fans and hard disk light may still show activity
Restarting leads back to the same stuck screen
possibleCauses: A recent Windows update did not finish installing correctly
A driver is preventing Windows from finishing startup
Corrupted system files
A failing hard drive struggling to read needed files
Startup program or service causing a hang
Malware interfering with the boot process
diagnosticQuestions: How long have you waited on this screen before assuming it is stuck?
Did this happen right after a Windows update was installing?
Did you add any new hardware or drivers recently?
Is the hard disk activity light blinking, indicating something is still happening, or is it completely idle?
Has this happened before, or is this the first time?

commands.purpose: Check the drive for errors that could be preventing Windows from reading needed startup files, run from Recovery Environment
commands.expectedResult: No errors found on the disk
commands.abnormalResult: Bad sectors or file errors found, which explains why Windows cannot finish loading

commands.purpose: Scan and repair corrupted system files, run from Recovery Environment command prompt with correct offline path if needed
commands.expectedResult: No integrity violations found, or found issues successfully repaired
commands.abnormalResult: Corrupt files found that could not be fixed, requiring further repair steps

troubleshootingSteps.action: Wait at least 15-20 minutes to rule out a slow but genuinely completing update installation
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Major Windows updates can sometimes take a long time to finish, especially on older or slower drives

troubleshootingSteps.action: Force a restart by holding the power button, then try starting normally again
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This tests if the previous startup attempt was a temporary glitch

troubleshootingSteps.action: If it happens again, force a restart three times in a row during the stuck screen to trigger Windows Automatic Repair environment
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Windows automatically detects repeated failed boots and offers recovery options

troubleshootingSteps.action: From the recovery environment, try Startup Repair first
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This automated tool can fix many common causes of a stuck boot process

troubleshootingSteps.action: If Startup Repair does not help, try booting into Safe Mode
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Safe Mode loads only essential drivers, helping determine if a specific driver or startup program is causing the hang

troubleshootingSteps.action: If Safe Mode works, uninstall recently added drivers or software from Safe Mode
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This removes the likely cause while keeping the rest of the system intact

troubleshootingSteps.action: Run chkdsk and sfc /scannow from the recovery command prompt
troubleshootingSteps.reason: These check for and repair disk errors and corrupted system files that could be blocking startup

possibleSolutions: Allow more time for a genuine update to finish
Run Startup Repair from Windows Recovery Environment
Boot into Safe Mode and remove a recently added driver or program
Repair disk errors using chkdsk
Repair system files using sfc /scannow
Roll back a recent Windows update if it caused the problem
prevention: Avoid interrupting Windows updates once they begin installing
Keep drivers updated from trusted sources only
Maintain regular backups in case a repair is not possible
Keep the hard drive healthy with regular checks

problem: Blue Screen of Death (BSOD) appears during startup or use
description: The computer suddenly displays a blue screen with white text and an error code, then restarts on its own. This can happen during Windows startup or at random times while using the computer.
symptoms: Blue screen with an error code such as 'CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED' or 'PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA'
Computer restarts automatically after the blue screen
May happen once, or repeatedly every time the computer starts
Sometimes shows a QR code or 'stop code' at the bottom of the screen
possibleCauses: A faulty or incompatible driver
Corrupted system files
Failing RAM or hard drive
A bad Windows update
Overheating hardware
Incompatible or corrupted software recently installed
diagnosticQuestions: What is the exact stop code or error name shown on the blue screen?
Does this happen during startup, or randomly while using the computer?
Did you install anything new right before this started, such as a driver, update, or hardware?
How often does this happen?

commands.purpose: Run Windows Memory Diagnostic to check for faulty RAM
commands.expectedResult: No memory problems detected
commands.abnormalResult: Memory errors found, pointing to faulty RAM as the cause

commands.purpose: Repair corrupted system files that could be causing instability
commands.expectedResult: No integrity violations found or issues repaired
commands.abnormalResult: Corrupt files found that cannot be repaired automatically

commands.purpose: Open Driver Verifier to stress-test drivers and identify which one is causing crashes
commands.expectedResult: Tool runs and helps narrow down a faulty driver over several restarts
commands.abnormalResult: System crashes more frequently while testing, which helps pinpoint the exact problem driver

troubleshootingSteps.action: Note the exact stop code or error name shown on the blue screen
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This code points toward the likely cause, such as memory, driver, or disk related problems

troubleshootingSteps.action: Think about what was recently installed or changed, such as new hardware, drivers, or software
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Most blue screens are triggered by a recent change rather than appearing out of nowhere

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the crash happens during startup, boot into Safe Mode
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Safe Mode avoids loading non-essential drivers, which helps confirm if a driver is the cause

troubleshootingSteps.action: From Safe Mode, uninstall recently added drivers or roll back a recent Windows update
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This removes the most likely cause of a sudden crash pattern

troubleshootingSteps.action: Run the Windows Memory Diagnostic tool to test for faulty RAM
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Bad memory is one of the most common hardware causes of blue screens

troubleshootingSteps.action: Run sfc /scannow to check for corrupted system files
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Damaged system files can cause instability that leads to crashes

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check the computer for overheating by inspecting fans and vents for dust buildup
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Overheating can cause sudden crashes as a safety measure to protect the hardware

troubleshootingSteps.action: Update all drivers, especially graphics and chipset, to the latest stable versions
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Outdated or buggy drivers are one of the most common overall causes of blue screens

possibleSolutions: Roll back or update the driver causing the crash
Replace faulty RAM
Repair corrupted system files
Clean dust to fix overheating
Uninstall a recently installed incompatible program
Reinstall Windows if the cause cannot be found
prevention: Keep drivers updated from official sources
Avoid installing unverified or pirated software
Clean the computer regularly to prevent overheating
Create restore points before major driver or software changes

problem: Black screen appears after logging into Windows
description: The user enters their password and the login screen disappears, but instead of the desktop appearing, the screen stays completely black, sometimes with just a mouse cursor visible.
symptoms: Screen goes black right after entering the password
Mouse cursor may still move on the black screen
No taskbar, icons, or desktop background appear
Ctrl+Alt+Delete may or may not bring up a menu
possibleCauses: The graphics driver crashed or failed to load
Windows Explorer (the process that draws the desktop) is not starting
A second monitor or display setting is confusing the display output
A corrupted user profile
A stuck Windows update installing in the background
A startup program interfering with the desktop loading
diagnosticQuestions: Does the mouse cursor move on the black screen, or is the whole computer frozen?
Does pressing Ctrl+Alt+Delete bring up any menu?
Are you using more than one monitor?
Did this start after a Windows update or driver installation?
Have you waited several minutes in case an update is finishing?

commands.purpose: Open Task Manager using Ctrl+Shift+Esc to check if Explorer.exe is running
commands.expectedResult: Task Manager opens and Explorer.exe is listed as running
commands.abnormalResult: Explorer.exe is missing from the process list, confirming the desktop process failed to start

commands.purpose: Manually restart the Windows Explorer process from Task Manager's Run new task option
commands.expectedResult: The desktop, taskbar, and icons appear normally
commands.abnormalResult: Explorer.exe fails to start or crashes again immediately, pointing to a deeper corruption issue

troubleshootingSteps.action: Wait a few minutes in case Windows is finishing an update installation in the background
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Some updates cause a temporary black screen while final setup steps complete

troubleshootingSteps.action: Try pressing Ctrl+Alt+Delete to see if a menu appears
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This confirms whether the computer is truly frozen or just failing to display the desktop

troubleshootingSteps.action: Open Task Manager using Ctrl+Shift+Esc and check if Explorer.exe is running
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Explorer.exe controls the desktop and taskbar, and if it is not running, nothing will display

troubleshootingSteps.action: If Explorer.exe is missing, go to File > Run new task in Task Manager and type explorer.exe
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This manually restarts the process responsible for showing the desktop

troubleshootingSteps.action: If using multiple monitors, try pressing Windows key + P to cycle through display modes
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Sometimes the display output is being sent to a monitor that is not currently active or connected

troubleshootingSteps.action: Update or roll back the graphics driver from Device Manager if accessible through Task Manager
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A crashed graphics driver is a common cause of a black screen after login

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the problem is specific to one user account, try logging in with a different account to test for profile corruption
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This helps determine if the issue is a broken user profile rather than a system-wide problem

troubleshootingSteps.action: Boot into Safe Mode if the black screen happens every time, to remove recently added startup programs or drivers
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Safe Mode bypasses non-essential drivers and startup items that could be causing the black screen

possibleSolutions: Restart the Explorer.exe process manually
Update or roll back the graphics driver
Switch display output mode using Windows key + P
Fix a corrupted user profile by creating a new one
Remove a problematic startup program from Safe Mode
Wait for a background update to finish
prevention: Keep graphics drivers updated
Avoid forcefully powering off during Windows updates
Maintain a backup local administrator account for troubleshooting
Regularly check for and install Windows updates in a controlled manner

problem: Login failed even with the correct password
description: The user enters what they believe is the correct username and password at the Windows login screen, but receives an error message saying the login information is incorrect.
symptoms: Message saying 'The password is incorrect' or 'Login attempt failed'
Password appears to be typed correctly but is still rejected
May happen with a local account or a Microsoft account
Account may show as locked after several attempts
possibleCauses: Caps Lock or Num Lock is on, changing what is actually typed
The user is mistakenly trying a different account's password
The password was recently changed on another device (for Microsoft accounts) and not yet updated locally
A keyboard layout mismatch causing wrong characters to be typed
The account is locked out after too many failed attempts
Account corruption or a Windows update sync issue with Microsoft accounts
diagnosticQuestions: Is Caps Lock or Num Lock currently turned on?
Is this a local Windows account or a Microsoft (online) account?
Did you recently change this password on another device or website?
Have you tried typing the password into a text box first to check for typing mistakes?
How many times have you tried logging in so far?

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check if Caps Lock or Num Lock is on, since this is often indicated by a small icon on the login screen
troubleshootingSteps.reason: An accidentally enabled Caps Lock is one of the most common reasons a correct password gets rejected

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm the correct keyboard layout is selected on the login screen
troubleshootingSteps.reason: A mismatched keyboard layout can cause certain keys to produce different characters than expected

troubleshootingSteps.action: Type the password into a visible text field, such as the search bar temporarily, to check it is being typed correctly (only if it is safe and private to do so)
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This helps rule out simple typing mistakes

troubleshootingSteps.action: If this is a Microsoft account, check if the password was changed recently on another device or through a browser
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Microsoft accounts sync passwords online, and a recent change elsewhere may not have updated on this specific computer yet, especially without internet access

troubleshootingSteps.action: Confirm you are logging into the correct account if multiple accounts exist on the computer
troubleshootingSteps.reason: It is common to accidentally try the password for a different account than the one selected

troubleshootingSteps.action: Wait a period of time if the account appears locked after several failed attempts
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Some account lockout policies require a waiting period or administrator action before allowing further attempts

troubleshootingSteps.action: Use the 'Reset password' or 'I forgot my password' link on the login screen if available
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This provides an official recovery path when the correct password truly cannot be recalled or is out of sync

possibleSolutions: Turn off Caps Lock or Num Lock before typing the password
Select the correct keyboard layout
Update the password using an internet connection if it was changed on another device
Select the correct user account before entering the password
Use the official password reset option
Contact an administrator to unlock the account
prevention: Use a password manager to avoid typing mistakes
Keep track of which account type is used, local or Microsoft
Update passwords consistently across devices
Set up a password reset method in advance, such as a recovery email or phone number

problem: Forgot Windows password and cannot log in
description: The user cannot remember their Windows password at all and has no way to log in normally, needing a way to reset it or regain access to the computer.
symptoms: User cannot recall the password for their account
No other working account is available on the computer
Login screen only offers the option to enter a password with no visible reset link
User may not know if the account is local or a Microsoft account
possibleCauses: Simply forgetting the password over time
Confusion between multiple accounts and their passwords
The account is a Microsoft account, and password reset requires internet access
The account is a local account with no recovery method set up
A previous password change was not properly remembered or recorded
diagnosticQuestions: Is this a local Windows account or a Microsoft account (an email address used to sign in)?
Do you have access to another administrator account on this same computer?
Do you have internet access available right now to reset a Microsoft account password?
Did you ever set up a password reset disk for this account?
Is there any written record or password manager where this password might be saved?

troubleshootingSteps.action: Determine whether the account is a Microsoft account (usually an email address) or a local account
troubleshootingSteps.reason: The recovery process is completely different depending on the account type

troubleshootingSteps.action: If it is a Microsoft account, use another device with internet access to visit the Microsoft account password reset page

Turn off Fast Startup

description: The computer stops responding to mouse clicks and keyboard input entirely, with the screen staying frozen in place, sometimes requiring a forced restart to recover.

troubleshootingSteps.action: If Task Manager opens and shows a specific program as 'Not Responding', end that program's task

troubleshootingSteps.action: If nothing responds at all, wait a short time in case the system is just extremely busy, before forcing a restart

troubleshootingSteps.action: After restarting, check Event Viewer for any error messages logged around the time of the freeze

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check if freezes happen during a specific activity, such as gaming or video editing, and monitor temperatures during that activity if possible

Clean dust and improve cooling to prevent overheating
Replace faulty RAM
Update graphics and chipset drivers
Remove malware

Keep drivers updated
Avoid running too many demanding programs at once

problem: High CPU usage is slowing down the computer
description: Task Manager shows the CPU usage staying very high, often near 100%, even when the user is not running demanding programs, causing the whole computer to feel slow and unresponsive.
symptoms: Task Manager shows CPU usage constantly near 100%
Fan runs loudly and continuously
Programs are slow to open or respond

A driver issue causing a process to use excessive CPU
Outdated hardware unable to keep up with current software demands
diagnosticQuestions: Does this happen all the time, or only during specific activities?
Have you checked Task Manager to see which specific process is using the most CPU?
Did this start suddenly, or has it been building up over time?
Have you installed any new software recently?

commands.purpose: Open Task Manager and sort processes by CPU usage to identify the exact cause

commands.purpose: Open Resource Monitor for more detailed information about CPU usage by process and service
commands.expectedResult: Shows a detailed breakdown of what is using CPU resources
commands.abnormalResult: A system process or unknown service consistently shows unusually high usage

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the top process is unfamiliar or oddly named, research it briefly or treat it as a potential malware concern
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Malware often disguises itself as a normal-sounding process to use system resources without detection

troubleshootingSteps.action: Run a full antivirus scan if malware is suspected
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This can detect and remove hidden malicious processes consuming CPU resources

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check if Windows Update or a system maintenance task is running in the background

troubleshootingSteps.action: Close unnecessary programs and browser tabs that may be contributing to overall CPU load

troubleshootingSteps.action: Update the driver related to the high-usage process if it appears to be a system or hardware-related service

possibleSolutions: Close or uninstall the specific program causing high usage
Remove malware found during a scan
Wait for legitimate background tasks like updates to finish
Update a driver linked to a high-usage system process
Upgrade hardware if it is simply outdated
Reduce the number of programs running simultaneously
prevention: Regularly monitor Task Manager to catch problems early
Keep antivirus software active and updated
Avoid installing unnecessary background programs
Keep drivers and Windows updated

Not enough physical RAM installed for current usage needs
Background programs and startup items using more memory than needed
Malware consuming memory resources
diagnosticQuestions: How many programs and browser tabs do you typically have open at the same time?
Does memory usage increase gradually the longer the computer stays on, or is it high right from startup?
How much total RAM does the computer have installed?
Have you noticed one specific program using an unusually large or growing amount of memory?

commands.purpose: Open Task Manager and sort processes by memory usage to find the biggest consumers
commands.expectedResult: Shows a clear list of which programs are using the most memory
commands.abnormalResult: A single process shows memory usage that keeps growing over time without the user doing anything new, suggesting a memory leak

troubleshootingSteps.action: Open Task Manager and sort the Processes tab by memory usage from highest to lowest

troubleshootingSteps.action: Close unnecessary programs and browser tabs that are not currently needed
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This is the fastest way to free up memory and improve responsiveness immediately

troubleshootingSteps.action: Watch if a specific program's memory usage keeps climbing steadily over time without the user doing anything new in it
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This pattern suggests a memory leak, where a program fails to release memory it no longer needs

troubleshootingSteps.action: If a memory leak is suspected in a specific program, close and reopen that program periodically, and check for updates to it
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Updates often fix known memory leak bugs, and restarting the program releases the leaked memory temporarily

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check the Startup tab in Task Manager and disable unnecessary startup programs

troubleshootingSteps.action: Run a full antivirus scan to rule out malware consuming memory

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check the total amount of RAM installed and compare it to what is typically recommended for the programs being used

possibleSolutions: Close unnecessary programs and browser tabs
Restart a program experiencing a memory leak
Update software with known memory leak issues
Disable unnecessary startup programs
Remove malware consuming memory
Add more physical RAM to the computer

Keep software updated to fix known memory leak bugs
Restart the computer regularly to clear accumulated memory usage
Monitor memory usage periodically to catch issues early

Windows Update downloading or installing in the background
A failing or very old, slow hard drive
Too many programs trying to read or write files at the same time

diagnosticQuestions: Does this happen all the time, or does it improve after leaving the computer running for a while?
Is this a traditional hard drive (HDD) or a solid state drive (SSD)?

commands.expectedResult: Services are running normally with reasonable resource use
commands.abnormalResult: One of these services correlates directly with spikes in disk activity

troubleshootingSteps.action: Open Task Manager and sort the Processes tab by disk usage to see what is causing the activity
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This identifies the exact process responsible for the high disk usage

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check if Windows Search indexing, an antivirus scan, or Windows Update is currently running

troubleshootingSteps.action: If the SysMain (Superfetch) service seems to be causing high disk usage, especially on an older hard drive, consider disabling it as a test

troubleshootingSteps.action: Check if this is a traditional hard drive (HDD) rather than an SSD

troubleshootingSteps.reason: A drive struggling with errors will show high usage while accomplishing very little actual work

troubleshootingSteps.action: Run a full antivirus and malware scan
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Some malware causes excessive, unnecessary disk activity

troubleshootingSteps.action: Consider upgrading from a hard disk drive to a solid state drive if the computer is old and disk usage remains consistently high

possibleSolutions: Wait for legitimate background tasks like indexing or updates to finish
Adjust Windows Search indexing settings
Disable the SysMain service if it is causing problems
Repair disk errors using chkdsk
Remove malware causing excessive disk activity
Upgrade to an SSD for significantly better performance
prevention: Keep the hard drive healthy with regular checks
Avoid running too many disk-intensive programs at once
Keep antivirus software updated and scheduled during idle times
Consider an SSD upgrade for aging computers

Run the Windows Update Troubleshooter

Temporarily disable third-party antivirus during the update

A registry cleaning tool reports finding many errors
possibleCauses: Leftover registry entries from improperly uninstalled software
Manual registry edits that were done incorrectly
Malware that has modified registry entries
A failed or interrupted software installation leaving incomplete registry data
General accumulation of outdated entries over a long period of use
diagnosticQuestions: What exact error message mentions the registry, and when does it appear?
Did you or anyone else recently make manual changes to the registry?
Did you recently uninstall software, and did the uninstall complete without errors?
Have you used any third-party registry cleaning tools recently?

commands.purpose: Check for and repair corrupted system files, which can sometimes resolve issues that appear registry-related but are actually deeper system file problems
commands.expectedResult: No integrity violations found, or issues successfully repaired
commands.abnormalResult: Corruption found that could not be repaired, suggesting more serious underlying damage

troubleshootingSteps.action: Note the exact error message and when it appears, such as during startup or when opening a specific program
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This helps pinpoint whether the issue is isolated to one program or affects the whole system

troubleshootingSteps.action: If a recent manual registry change was made, undo that specific change if it can be identified
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Manual registry edits are one of the most direct and identifiable causes of new registry-related problems

troubleshootingSteps.action: Use System Restore to return to a point before the problem started, if a suitable restore point is available
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This safely reverts registry changes without needing to manually identify and fix each individual entry

troubleshootingSteps.action: Run sfc /scannow to check for and repair corrupted system files, since some symptoms that seem registry-related are actually caused by file corruption
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This addresses a related but different type of system-level problem that can produce similar symptoms

troubleshootingSteps.action: Uninstall and reinstall the specific program associated with the error, if the problem is limited to one application
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This replaces any incomplete or corrupted registry entries left behind by a previous faulty installation or uninstallation

troubleshootingSteps.action: Run a full antivirus scan to rule out malware that may have modified registry entries
troubleshootingSteps.reason: Some malware directly edits the registry to achieve persistence or disable security features

troubleshootingSteps.action: Avoid using aggressive third-party registry cleaning tools, since they can sometimes remove entries that are actually needed, causing new problems
troubleshootingSteps.reason: These tools are not always reliable and can occasionally cause more harm than good if used carelessly

troubleshootingSteps.action: As a last resort for severe, widespread registry corruption, consider a full reinstall of Windows
troubleshootingSteps.reason: This guarantees a completely clean, correctly structured registry when other targeted repairs are not sufficient

possibleSolutions: Undo a recent manual registry change
Use System Restore to revert to a working state
Repair system files using sfc /scannow
Reinstall the specific program causing registry-related errors
Remove malware that modified the registry
Reinstall Windows for severe, widespread corruption
prevention: Avoid manual registry edits unless you fully understand the change being made
Always back up the registry before making manual changes
Use official uninstall methods rather than simply deleting program folders
Keep antivirus software active and updated
Avoid aggressive third-party registry cleaning tools
